summary: Updates RFC 3370 to describe how to use the SHAKE family of hash functions in the Cryptographic Message Syntax with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA. It also describes conventions for the associated signer public keys.

eli5.summary: Signing a message first boils it down with a hash. This adds a newer boiling method, SHAKE, to the options for signed messages.

subtitle: How to use the SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 hash functions for digests, signatures and MACs in signed and authenticated CMS messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) had no standard way to name or use the SHAKE hash functions from the SHA-3 family, which can produce output of any length.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8702 lists the object identifiers to use and fixes the output length for each use: 32 bytes for SHAKE128 and 64 bytes for SHAKE256. It also sets the rules for RSASSA-PSS signatures, ECDSA signatures, public keys and KMAC message authentication codes.
tldr.outcome: CMS implementations can use SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 with RSASSA-PSS, ECDSA and KMAC in a uniform way. The RFC updates RFC 3370 and is a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 8702 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3370, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is the format used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message contents. RFC 3370 defines how common algorithms are used with it. RFC 8702 updates RFC 3370 to add SHAKE128 and SHAKE256, taken from the SHA-3 standard, as hash functions in CMS.

It covers their use with the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) in the CMS signed-data content type. A SHAKE can serve as the message digest function, as the message authentication code, and as the mask generation function in RSASSA-PSS. Four other SHA-3 instances (SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512) are out of scope.
sections.eli5: People already sign messages with a hash-and-sign recipe. This RFC adds two new hash ingredients to the recipe book and explains how to use them in signatures and checks.

sections.title: What a SHAKE Is
sections.content:
In the SHA-3 family, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 are extendable-output functions. A SHAKE is a variable-length hash function written SHAKE(M, d), where the output is a d-bit digest of message M. The RFC gives the collision resistance of SHAKE128 as min(d/2,128) bits and of SHAKE256 as min(d/2,256) bits, with second-preimage resistance of min(d,128) and min(d,256) bits.

Because the output length can vary, CMS has to pick one. This specification uses d=256 for SHAKE128 and d=512 for SHAKE256, which is 32 and 64 bytes.
sections.eli5: Most hash machines always give the same size fingerprint. A SHAKE can give any size you ask for, so the RFC simply picks one size for each of the two kinds.

sections.title: Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight object identifiers (OIDs). Two name the hash functions themselves: id-shake128 and id-shake256, defined by NIST. Two come from RFC 8692 and name RSASSA-PSS with a SHAKE: id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 and id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256. Two more from RFC 8692 name ECDSA with a SHAKE: id-ecdsa-with-shake128 and id-ecdsa-with-shake256. The last two, id-KmacWithSHAKE128 and id-KmacWithSHAKE256, name Keccak message authentication codes (KMAC).

For the hash, RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA identifiers, the parameters MUST be absent, so the identifier is a SEQUENCE of one component, the OID. For the two KMAC identifiers the parameters are OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: Each method gets its own long number, like a library call number. For most of them the number says everything, so no extra notes are allowed.

sections.title: Digests in CMS
sections.content:
The id-shake128 and id-shake256 OIDs can be used as the digest algorithm identifiers in the SignedData, SignerInfo, DigestedData and AuthenticatedData digestAlgorithm fields. The encoding MUST omit the parameters field, and the output length MUST be 32 bytes for SHAKE128 and 64 bytes for SHAKE256.

The digest algorithm MUST be the same as the message hash algorithm used in the signature.
sections.eli5: Wherever a message says which fingerprint machine it used, it can now name SHAKE. The fingerprint must be the standard size, and the signature has to use the same machine.

sections.title: RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA Signatures
sections.content:
For RSASSA-PSS, the parameters are omitted because the hash, mask generation algorithm, trailer and salt are embedded in the OID. The hash and the mask generation function MUST be the same SHAKE: both SHAKE128 or both SHAKE256. The SHAKE is used natively as the mask generation function instead of MGF1. Its output length is (8*emLen - 264) bits for SHAKE128 or (8*emLen - 520) bits for SHAKE256. For a 2048-bit RSA modulus that is 1784 or 1528 bits. The saltLength MUST be 32 bytes for SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for SHAKE256, and the trailerField MUST be 1, meaning the hexadecimal value 0xBC.

For ECDSA, the identifier also omits parameters, and the SHAKE output length MUST be 32 or 64 bytes. Certification authorities generating ECDSA with SHAKE signatures in certificates or CRLs SHOULD use a deterministic, nonrandom k as in RFC 6979.

The RSA modulus or ECDSA curve order SHOULD be chosen in line with the SHAKE output length.
sections.eli5: A signature has several settings, such as the size of the salt and which mixing machine to use. The OID fixes all of them in advance, so nobody has to send them along.

sections.title: Public Keys
sections.content:
The signer's public key algorithm identifier goes in the algorithm attribute of the OriginatorPublicKey. The encoding follows RFC 3279, RFC 4055 and RFC 5480.

The rsaEncryption OID still identifies an RSA key when the owner does not want to limit it to RSASSA-PSS with SHAKEs. If the owner wants that limit, the RSASSA-PSS identifier SHOULD be used. For ECDSA with SHAKE public keys, implementations MUST name the algorithms explicitly with the OIDs from Section 2. The identifier parameters MUST be absent.
sections.eli5: A public key can carry a label saying it is only for one kind of signing. Using the label is a good idea if you want to stop the key being used any other way.

sections.title: Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
KMAC is the Keccak message authentication code. In CMS, its identifier goes in the AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field and its value in the mac field. When the parameters are absent, the output length used is 32 bytes for id-KmacWithSHAKE128 and 64 bytes for id-KmacWithSHAKE256, and the customization string is empty. When computing KMAC the variable N is 0xD2B282C2, S is an empty string, and L is 256 or 512 bits.

Implementations that process KMACs with the SHAKEs MUST recognize these identifiers.
sections.eli5: A MAC is a secret-handshake stamp that proves a message was not changed. KMAC is a stamp made with SHAKE.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3370 apply here too. SHAKE128 with a 32-byte output offers 128 bits of collision and preimage resistance, so its OIDs are RECOMMENDED with a 2048-bit (112-bit security) or 3072-bit (128-bit security) RSA modulus, or with curves whose group order is 256 bits. SHAKE256 with a 64-byte output offers 256 bits, so its OIDs are RECOMMENDED with a 4096-bit or larger RSA modulus, or curves with a group order of at least 512 bits, such as NIST curve P-521.

The RFC adds that 256 bits of security from RSA would need a 15360-bit modulus, which is impractical. Finally, when more than two parties share the same message-authentication key, data origin authentication is not provided, since any of them can compute a valid MAC.
sections.eli5: A strong lock on a weak door does not help. Pick key sizes that match the strength of the hash.
